newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir engineer takes strain on maiden space flight.
newsitem.headline: Mir engineer takes strain on maiden space flight.

text.p: Mir flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin returned from his first space mission on Thursday looking more shattered than his commander, who drew the limelight during their rocky six months in orbit.
Lazutkin remained in the background for most of his time on Mir, overshadowed by crew commander Vasily Tsibliyev and NASA astronaut Michael Foale.
On Thursday, true to tradition, he was carried out of the Soyuz capsule several minutes after Tsibliyev, who was immediately surrounded by doctors and officials.
Lazutkin came out smiling, but appeared to have less energy than his boss, who doctors feared might need special treatment for an irregular heartbeat he got after a crash on Mir in June.
Asked how he felt, the unassuming, moustachioed 39-year-old engineer said: "Basically okay, after the flight. I thought it would have been worse."
Space officials said it was not surprising Lazutkin looked tired. Few cosmonauts have had such a baptism of fire -- literally -- on their first mission.
Within days of his arrival on Mir in February, he had to deal with a serious blaze which broke out on the station.

While scientific colleagues were frustrated by a series of mishaps, some of them nearly fatal, Lazutkin, with help from his crewmates and ground control, pushed back the frontiers of human experience of emergency repair work in space.

In July, after one tired crew member accidentally pulled the plug on one of Mir's computers, plunging the ship into darkness, it was Lazutkin who worked round the clock to crank the ship back to life as his crewmates slept.

If humankind goes on exploring the cosmos, then more astronauts will have to cope with the sort of repeated problems like fires and oxygen-system breakdowns, leaks, collisions and computer crashes that "Sasha" Lazutkin has had to deal with.

His training as a competitive gymnast may have been as important for him as years working as an engineer at the Soviet Energia rocket company when it came to tackling long and arduous repairs aboard the 11-year-old Mir, which is showing its age.

Lazutkin, a married man with two daughters, faced the most hazardous and demanding task following the June 25 accident when an unmanned craft being manoeuvred by Tsibliyev collided with and punctured the Spektr module.
But he was pulled from the risky and complicated job repairing Spektr after both he and Tsibliyev were deemed too tired to deal with any more problems.
One person who had no doubts about Lazutkin's ability to stand the strain was Oleg Grachev, head of Moscow's Olympic Sport School No. 51, where the cosmonaut was a budding teenage gymnast.
"He was a very disciplined," Grachev told Reuters. "Quiet, serious and always with his mind on his lessons."

Lazutkin would probably modestly agree with mission director Vladimir Solovyov's refusal to call him the hero of the day on Friday: "We only have heroes of the day on television. It was all in a day's work for the flight engineer."
